T2.1.1.desc: Define a market; local, national and international markets; product and resource markets

T2.1.2.desc: Outline the meaning of a competitive market (competition vs market power)

T2.2.1.desc: Explain the law of demand (individual demand, ceteris paribus, demand schedule)

T2.2.3.desc: Explain the relationship between individual demand and market demand

T2.2.4.desc: Analyse the non-price determinants of demand as causes of demand curve shifts

T2.2.5.desc: Using diagrams, distinguish between movements along and shifts of the demand curve

T2.2.6.desc: (HL) Assumptions underlying the law of demand: the law of diminishing marginal utility

T2.2.7.desc: (HL) Assumptions underlying the law of demand: the income and substitution effects

T2.3.1.desc: Explain the law of supply (individual supply, supply schedule)

T2.3.2.desc: Draw a supply curve (including the vertical supply curve)

T2.3.3.desc: Explain the relationship between individual supply and market supply

T2.3.4.desc: Analyse the non-price determinants of supply as causes of supply curve shifts

T2.3.5.desc: Using diagrams, distinguish between movements along and shifts of the supply curve

T2.3.6.desc: (HL) Assumptions underlying the law of supply: the law of diminishing marginal returns

T2.3.7.desc: (HL) Assumptions underlying the law of supply: increasing marginal costs and the firm's supply curve

T2.4.1.desc: Draw a diagram to illustrate how demand and supply interact to determine market equilibrium

T2.4.2.desc: Analyse demand and supply curve shifts that give rise to a new equilibrium, using excess demand (shortage) and excess supply (surplus)

T2.4.3.desc: Draw diagrams to illustrate how shifts in demand and supply give rise to a new equilibrium (incl. free and economic goods)

T2.5.1.desc: Analyse the price mechanism: resource allocation through the signalling and incentive functions of prices

T2.5.2.desc: Analyse the price mechanism: rationing (price and non-price rationing)

T2.5.3.desc: Explain consumer surplus, producer surplus and social (community) surplus (MB and MC interpretation of demand and supply)

T2.5.4.desc: Draw a diagram showing maximum social surplus at competitive market equilibrium

T2.5.5.desc: Explain the conditions for allocative efficiency at competitive market equilibrium (MB = MC, maximum social surplus) and why intervention may still be needed

T2.6.1.desc: Evaluate the assumptions of consumer rationality, utility maximisation and perfect information

T2.6.2.desc: Behavioural critique: biases (rules of thumb, anchoring, framing, availability)

T2.6.3.desc: Behavioural critique: bounded rationality, bounded self-control, bounded selfishness, imperfect information

T2.6.4.desc: Policies inspired by behavioural economics: nudge theory

T2.6.5.desc: Policies inspired by behavioural economics: choice architecture (default, restricted and mandated choice)

T2.6.6.desc: Evaluate behavioural economics and its policies (mainstream response, advantages, disadvantages)

T2.6.8.desc: Alternative business objectives: corporate social responsibility, market share, growth, satisficing (and revenue maximisation)

T3.1.1.desc: Define PED and identify the various degrees and range of values for PED (sign, use of percentages)

T3.1.2.desc: Draw diagrams showing the range of values for PED (relatively elastic and inelastic; perfectly elastic, perfectly inelastic, unitary) and PED versus steepness

T3.1.3.desc: (HL) Explain and illustrate changing PED along a straight-line downward-sloping demand curve

T3.1.5.desc: Explain the relationship between PED and total revenue

T3.1.6.desc: Draw a diagram to show how total revenue changes in response to a price change with elastic, inelastic or unit elastic demand

T3.1.7.desc: Apply PED: its importance for firms (pricing) and government decision-making (indirect taxes)

T3.1.8.desc: (HL) Analyse why primary commodities generally have a lower PED than manufactured products (and the consequences for prices and producer revenues)

T3.2.1.desc: Define YED and, depending on the sign of YED, distinguish between normal and inferior goods

T3.2.2.desc: Depending on the value of YED (less than or greater than one), distinguish between necessities, luxuries and services

T3.2.3.desc: Draw an Engel curve diagram to show income elastic, income inelastic and inferior goods

T3.2.4.desc: (HL) Apply YED: discuss its relevance to firms

T3.2.5.desc: (HL) Apply YED: discuss changes in the sectoral structure of an economy

T3.3.1.desc: Define PES and identify the various degrees and range of values for PES

T3.3.2.desc: Draw diagrams showing the range of values for PES (relatively elastic and inelastic; perfectly elastic, perfectly inelastic, unitary)

T3.3.4.desc: (HL) Apply PES: why primary commodities generally have a lower PES than manufactured products (and the consequences)

T4.1.1.desc: Outline key reasons why governments intervene in markets (incl. the Real world issue 2 overview)

T4.1.2.desc: Outline the forms government intervention takes at the microeconomic level

T4.2.1.desc: Price controls: meaning, and why they cause persistent market disequilibrium

T4.2.2.desc: Price ceilings: explain and draw the consequences for markets (shortage, non-price rationing, underground markets, underallocation, welfare loss)

T4.2.3.desc: Price ceilings: consequences for stakeholders and evaluation (incl. rent controls and food price controls)

T4.2.4.desc: Price floors for agricultural products: explain and draw the consequences for markets (surplus, government purchases, firm inefficiency, overallocation, welfare loss)

T4.2.5.desc: Price floors for agricultural products: consequences for stakeholders and evaluation

T4.2.6.desc: Minimum wages: explain and draw the consequences for the economy and stakeholders, and evaluate

T4.3.1.desc: The meaning of indirect taxes: excise and general taxes, indirect versus direct, specific versus ad valorem

T4.3.2.desc: Indirect taxes and resource allocation; why governments impose indirect taxes

T4.3.3.desc: Draw diagrams and explain the impacts of a specific tax on market outcomes

T4.3.4.desc: Explain the consequences of indirect taxes for stakeholders

T4.3.5.desc: Evaluate indirect taxes: consumer and producer surplus, welfare loss and allocative inefficiency

T4.4.1.desc: The meaning of subsidies; subsidies and the allocation of resources

T4.4.2.desc: Why governments grant subsidies (and why subsidies are controversial)

T4.4.3.desc: Draw diagrams and explain the impacts of a subsidy on market outcomes

T4.4.4.desc: Explain the consequences of subsidies for stakeholders

T4.4.5.desc: Evaluate subsidies: consumer and producer surplus, welfare loss and allocative inefficiency

T5.1.1.desc: Explain the meaning of common pool resources in terms of rivalry and non-excludability

T5.1.2.desc: Explain the tragedy of the commons

T5.1.3.desc: Explain the meaning of sustainable and unsustainable production (maximum sustainable yield; renewable and non-renewable resources)

T5.2.1.desc: Explain market failure as the failure of the market to achieve allocative efficiency

T5.2.2.desc: Explain that socially optimum output is produced when MSC = MSB and social surplus is maximum (MPB, MSB, MPC, MSC)

T5.2.3.desc: Draw a diagram illustrating allocative efficiency and socially optimum output

T5.2.4.desc: Explain the meaning of externalities as an example of market failure

T5.3.1.desc: Explain negative externalities of production (MSC above MPC) and the resulting overallocation

T5.3.2.desc: Explain and draw the welfare loss from negative production externalities

T5.3.3.desc: Explain that negative production externalities can illustrate the overuse of common pool resources

T5.3.6.desc: Government responses: tradable permits / cap and trade (explain, diagram)

T5.3.7.desc: Evaluate market-based policies (measurement difficulties, effectiveness, stakeholders; carbon taxes versus tradable permits)

T5.3.8.desc: Government responses: legislation and regulation (explain, diagram, evaluate)

T5.3.10.desc: Government responses: education and awareness creation (explain, evaluate)

T5.4.1.desc: Explain negative externalities of consumption (MSB below MPB) and the resulting overallocation

T5.4.2.desc: Explain and draw the welfare loss from negative consumption externalities

T5.4.3.desc: Negative consumption externalities and the overuse of common pool resources

T5.4.4.desc: Explain the meaning of demerit goods

T5.4.5.desc: Government responses: indirect (Pigouvian) taxes (explain, diagram, evaluate)

T5.4.6.desc: Government responses: legislation and regulation (explain, diagram, evaluate)

T5.4.7.desc: Government responses: education and awareness creation (explain, evaluate)

T5.4.9.desc: Evaluate policies for negative consumption externalities overall (combining policies; sugar taxes)

T6.1.1.desc: Explain positive externalities of production (MSC below MPC) and the resulting underallocation

T6.1.2.desc: Explain and draw the welfare loss from positive production externalities

T6.1.3.desc: Government responses: direct government provision and subsidies (explain, diagram)

T6.2.1.desc: Explain positive externalities of consumption (MSB above MPB) and the resulting underallocation

T6.2.2.desc: Explain and draw the welfare loss from positive consumption externalities

T6.2.3.desc: Explain the meaning of merit goods (reasons for underprovision)

T6.2.4.desc: Government responses that raise demand: legislation and regulation, education and awareness creation, nudges (explain, diagram)

T6.2.5.desc: Government responses that raise supply: direct government provision and subsidies (explain, diagram)

T6.2.6.desc: Evaluate policies to correct positive production and consumption externalities

T6.2.7.desc: Summary of externalities and rules for drawing externality diagrams

T6.3.1.desc: Explain public goods as non-rivalrous and non-excludable (and classify private goods, common pool resources, public and quasi-public goods)

T6.3.2.desc: Explain the free rider problem and why the market fails to provide public goods

T6.3.3.desc: Evaluate direct government provision of public goods (incl. cost-benefit analysis)

T6.3.4.desc: Evaluate contracting out the provision of public goods to the private sector

T6.4.1.desc: Explain asymmetric information and distinguish between adverse selection and moral hazard

T6.4.2.desc: Adverse selection (sellers know more): evaluate government responses (regulation, provision of information, licensure)

T6.4.3.desc: Adverse selection (sellers know more): evaluate private responses (screening and signalling)

T6.4.4.desc: Adverse selection (buyers know more, e.g. health insurance): private and government responses

T6.5.1.desc: Explain why the free market results in an unequal distribution of income (equity and equality; factor ownership and factor prices)

T6.5.2.desc: Draw a circular flow of income diagram to show why free markets give rise to income inequalities

T6.5.3.desc: Explain inequalities in wealth (income versus wealth) and how inequality relates to market failure

T7.1.1.desc: Explain the meaning of market power and its link to market failure (firms, industries, market structures)

T7.1.2.desc: Explain the main characteristics of perfect competition (many firms, free entry, homogeneous products)

T7.1.3.desc: Explain the main characteristics of monopoly (single or dominant firm, high barriers to entry, no close substitutes)

T7.1.4.desc: Explain the characteristics of imperfect competition: monopolistic competition (many firms, free entry, product differentiation)

T7.1.5.desc: Explain the characteristics of imperfect competition: oligopoly (few large firms, high barriers to entry, interdependence)

T7.1.6.desc: Compare the four market structures (market power versus competition) and explain why perfect competition is studied

T7.2.1.desc: Explain revenue concepts: total, average and marginal revenue (price takers versus price makers)

T7.2.2.desc: Explain cost concepts: economic (explicit and implicit) costs; total, average and marginal cost in the short run

T7.2.3.desc: Explain long-run costs: the long-run average cost curve, economies and diseconomies of scale

T7.2.4.desc: Explain profit concepts: economic profit, abnormal profit, normal profit, loss

T7.2.5.desc: Explain profit maximisation (MR = MC; total revenue minus total cost)

T7.3.1.desc: Explain firms in perfect competition as price takers with no market power (P = D = AR = MR)

T7.3.2.desc: Explain and draw short-run profit maximisation (abnormal profit, normal profit, loss)

T7.3.3.desc: Explain and draw long-run profit maximisation and equilibrium (normal profit through entry and exit)

T7.3.4.desc: Explain allocative efficiency in perfect competition (P = MC, MB = MC, maximum social surplus)

T7.3.5.desc: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of perfect competition

T7.4.1.desc: Explain barriers to entry (economies of scale, natural monopoly, branding, legal barriers, control of essential resources, aggressive tactics)

T7.4.2.desc: Explain the monopolist's demand and revenue curves and market power (AR above MC; P greater than MC)

T7.4.3.desc: Explain and draw profit maximisation by the monopolist (abnormal profit, normal profit, loss)

T7.4.5.desc: Explain the monopolist's allocative inefficiency and welfare loss compared with perfect competition (higher price, lower output)

T7.4.6.desc: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of monopoly

T7.5.1.desc: Explain the assumptions of monopolistic competition and the methods of product differentiation

T7.5.2.desc: Explain that monopolistic competition has less market power than monopoly (more elastic demand curve); price and non-price competition

T7.5.3.desc: Explain and draw profit maximisation in the short run and long run (abnormal profit, normal profit, loss)

T7.5.4.desc: Explain allocative inefficiency and market failure; more product variety in exchange for less efficiency

T7.5.5.desc: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of monopolistic competition (compared with perfect competition and monopoly)

T7.6.1.desc: Explain the characteristics of oligopoly (few large firms, high barriers to entry, interdependence)

T7.6.2.desc: Explain features of oligopoly: interdependence, strategic behaviour, incentive to collude versus incentive to cheat, risk of price war

T7.6.3.desc: Explain the simple game theory payoff matrix (prisoner's dilemma, Nash equilibrium)

T7.6.4.desc: Explain the relevance of price and non-price competition in oligopoly

T7.6.5.desc: Explain collusive oligopoly and draw a diagram (cartels, difficulties of maintaining them, informal collusion and price leadership)

T7.6.6.desc: Distinguish non-collusive oligopoly (strategic behaviour and price rigidity)

T7.6.7.desc: Explain market concentration and concentration ratios (and their weaknesses)

T7.6.8.desc: Explain allocative inefficiency and market failure in oligopoly; discuss its advantages and disadvantages

T7.7.1.desc: Discuss advantages of large firms with significant market power (economies of scale, R&D, innovation) and risks to output, price and consumer choice

T7.7.2.desc: Explain the meaning of abuse of market power (anti-competitive practices) and where it arises

T7.7.3.desc: Evaluate legislation and regulation to protect competition (competition policy, mergers)

T7.7.4.desc: Evaluate fines as a response to abuse of market power

T7.7.5.desc: Evaluate government ownership and regulation of natural monopolies (marginal cost and average cost pricing)
